transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52m
Attendees: Jordan Meyers (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Liam Chen (IvaAI CTO), Sofia Martinez (IvaAI ML Eng), Noah Park (IvaAI Infra), Amira Gomez (IvaAI PM)

Summary: quick pilot econ check: tokens/sec/$, caching wins, and tradeoffs between batching for cost and latency. Customer slightly worried about tail latency when batching; want clear next steps to validate cost model and a short benchmark with KV/prefix caching enabled.

Topics: cost per token, tokens per second per GPU, KV cache vs prefix cache, batching windows, p95/p99 latency behavior, hosted vs dedicated placement for pilot, quantization impact on throughput.

[00:00] Jordan: alright folks, thanks for joining, um 15:00 on our side, appreciate you making time. we'll do a quick run-through of the numbers, then dig into the latency question and next steps.
[00:18] Liam: yep thanks, quick note: we had a weird spike yesterday in staging, p99 jumped to like 2.1s which is outta our SLAs so wanna understand if that's batching or something else.
[00:30] Priya: okay noted — when you say spike, is that during higher qps or steady?
[00:35] Liam: mostly during bursts, the tail seems to get worse. average is fine.
[00:40] Priya: gotcha. so for context, the pilot runs a mix of short completions (30-50 tokens) and occasional long summarizations (~800 tokens) — that distribution matters for batching decisions.
[00:55] Sofia: yes that's our mix, and on weekdays we have a higher spike rate.
[01:02] Jordan: cool. I pulled the preliminary tokens/sec/$ sheet — overall we see about 12k tokens per dollar on the default hosted config with small batching (20ms window). if we increase batching to 80ms we get to ~18k tokens/$ but p95 increases ~40-60ms on average and p99 can pop.
[01:26] Noah: any numbers for Dedicated? if we reserved a pool, are those numbers better?
[01:31] Priya: Dedicated tends to improve predictable throughput — for the specific A100-like pool we estimated ~22-24k tokens/$ with similar batching, but that's assuming full utilization. important caveat: Dedicated is only worth it if you can sustain steady qps, otherwise burst costs and inefficiencies creep in.
[01:58] Amira: also curious about KV cache — we read the docs but want real numbers: how much can we save on tokens for our summarization flow?
[02:07] Priya: preliminary KV prefix caching numbers we ran on a similar workload showed ~25-35% token savings for repeated document contexts. for truly unique docs it's obviously less. the big win is when your requests share prefixes or retrieval contexts.
[02:26] Jordan: I'll add those ranges to the workbook, note that caching also reduces egress tokens and CPU overhead on the app side.
[02:34] Liam: question — when cache is warm, does latency improve or degrade with caching?
[02:39] Priya: warm cache usually reduces latency because you avoid re-encoding large chunks, but there's a tradeoff — cache lookups add a small constant, and if cache miss rates are high you pay both for lookup + full generation which can hurt.
[02:53] Sofia: hmm that matches what we saw; on one run warm cache cut p50 by ~80ms, p95 by ~200ms. but in some cases p99 was unchanged because of cold fetches from storage.
[03:07] Jordan: ok, next: quantization. small quant goes up throughput by ~15% but can increase token rejection for some sensitive prompts — that affects quality and re-generation. we should run evals.
[03:23] Priya: yes, we recommend keeping a validation prompt set during quantization tests so you see regression signals.
[03:29] Liam: do you have a short checklist for the experiments we should run?
[03:33] Priya: sure — 1) baseline run (no batching change, no cache), 2) batching window sweep (20/40/80/120ms), 3) KV warm vs cold tests, 4) quantization A/B with eval prompts, 5) Dedicated vs hosted synthetic load to compare tokens/sec/$.
[03:51] Amira: perfect. can we also get a breakdown by prompt type? the chat prompts are worst for tail latency.
[03:57] Jordan: yes we'll add prompt-type filters to the workbook.
[04:01] Noah: one infra note — our autoscaler has a min pod count of 3 and max 12, scaling is slow (30-60s). could that cause tail issues?
[04:10] Priya: absolutely — if the system relies on instance spin-up during a burst, you'll see added latency. for pilot we often recommend warming or higher minimums. also consider prewarmed connectors for heavy events.
[04:22] Liam: ok, so recommended short-term mitigation is bump min pods and tune batching?
[04:28] Priya: yes and enable prefix KV caching for hot documents; that combo usually gives the best cost/latency tradeoff for mixed workloads.
[04:37] Jordan: i ran a quick calc: with prefix caching warm and batching at 40ms we estimate effective tokens/$ ~20k and p95 under target in most cases. but if cache hit rate drops under 30% the economics degrade below hosted baseline.
[04:54] Sofia: what's the sensitivity on cache hit rate — like break-even point?
[04:58] Priya: rough break-even around 30-35% hit rate for their workload; below that we lean towards smaller batching and relying on dedicated throughput.
[05:07] Liam: any risk with data residency or security on caching? we can't persist certain PII.
[05:12] Jordan: yes we discussed that earlier — Redwood supports configurable TTLs, encryption-at-rest, and we can scope caches to not index sensitive fields. we'll share security docs.
[05:22] Liam: good. also curious about costs for long-run summarizations — 800 token outputs — does batching help there?
[05:27] Priya: batching helps less for very long outputs because generation time dominates; batching is most effective when you have many short requests to pack into a single forward. for long outputs, KV cache and model selection (smaller model for summarization or quantized variant) drive cost.
[05:44] Jordan: we can test rerouting long jobs to a quantized variant and measure quality delta; that often gives 20-30% cost savings with acceptable quality in many cases.
[05:55] Noah: for the Dedicated test, how do we provision without an enterprise contract? can we get a short-term reserved pool?
[05:59] Jordan: we can do a limited dedicated-style allocation for the pilot under a time-boxed arrangement — we'll propose specifics in the workbook and pricing note.
[06:08] Amira: okay next, pricing ask — can you show us tokens/sec/$ vs p95/p99 in a chart so execs can see tradeoffs?
[06:15] Jordan: yes I'll add charts.
[06:18] Sofia: one more question: does batching affect determinism for prompts with function calls? we've seen ordering issues.
[06:24] Priya: function-calling can be sensitive — batching is safe but you must ensure the runtime preserves per-request context and ordering; Redwood's engine isolates calls but there are edge cases with streamed function callbacks where latency might be slightly higher. we should test your function-heavy flows specifically.
[06:43] Liam: all right. anything else?
[06:45] Jordan: quick recap, we will: 1) share cost workbook with tokens/sec/$ and charts, 2) run KV cache and batching sweep experiments, 3) run quantization A/B with validation set, 4) propose a short dedicated-style test and pricing. we'll sync on results next week.
[06:59] Sofia: sounds good.
[07:01] Jordan: ok we'll follow up with timings. thanks everyone.

Notes / artifacts referenced: cost_workbook_link: https://redwood.workbooks/pilot/ivaai-costs (shared after call), security whitepaper link (redwood/security-pilot.pdf), pilot benchmark script repo: github.com/redwood/pilot-bench (note: spelling/links may be fuzzy in transcript).

Closing: approximate time 15:52 UTC.
